title: V. Elders
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, underdeveloped creature, a pale, consumptive dreamer. Quite the opposite: at this time Alyosha was a sturdy, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, glowing with health. He was very handsome, too. He was graceful and moderately tall, with dark brown hair and a regular, rather long, oval face. His dark gray eyes were wide-set and shining. He was very thoughtful and seemed very serene. I will be told, perhaps, that red cheeks do not rule out fanaticism and mysticism. But I think Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Oh, no doubt in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles are never a stumbling block to a realist. It is not miracles that lead realists to belief. The true realist, if he is an unbeliever, will always find the strength and ability to disbelieve in the miraculous. Faced with a miracle as an undeniable fact, he would sooner doubt his own senses than accept it. And if he does accept it, he accepts it as a fact of nature that he had simply not recognized before. In the realist, faith does not spring from the miracle; the miracle springs from faith. Once a realist believes, his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous too. The Apostle Thomas said he would not believe until he saw, but when he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not. He believed only because he wanted to believe, and perhaps in his secret heart he fully believed even when he said, “I do not believe till I see.”

I will be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, that he had not finished his studies, and so on. It is true that he did not finish his studies, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I will simply repeat what I said above. He chose this path only because at that time it alone struck his imagination, and it offered his soul an ideal escape from darkness into light. Add to that that he was, to some extent, a young man of our last epoch. That is, he was honest by nature. He wanted the truth, sought it and believed in it, and wanted to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul. He looked for immediate action and was ready to sacrifice everything for it, even life itself. Unfortunately, these young men fail to understand that sacrificing one’s life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices, and that to sacrifice, for instance, five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study, if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set as their goal, is a sacrifice utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he thought seriously, he was convinced that God and immortality exist, and at once he said to himself, instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise.” In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question. It is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form atheism takes today, the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to climb from earth to heaven but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”

Alyosha said to himself: “I can’t give two roubles instead of ‘all,’ and only go to mass instead of ‘following Him.’” Perhaps his childhood memories drew him to our monastery, where his mother may once have taken him to mass. Perhaps the slanting sunlight and the holy image his poor “crazy” mother had held him up to still worked on his imagination. Brooding on these things, he may have come to us only to find out whether here he could sacrifice everything, or only “two roubles.” And in the monastery he met this elder. I must digress here to explain what an “elder” is in Russian monasteries, and I am sorry to say I do not feel very competent to do so. I will try, however, to give a superficial account in a few words. Authorities on the subject assert that the institution of “elders” is recent, not more than a hundred years old in our monasteries, though in the Orthodox East, especially on Sinai and Athos, it has existed for over a thousand years. It is maintained that it existed in ancient times in Russia too. But then came the calamities that befell Russia—the Tartars, civil war, the break in relations with the East after the fall of Constantinople—and the institution fell into oblivion. It was revived among us toward the end of the last century by one of the great “ascetics,” as they called him, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his disciples. Even today it exists in only a few monasteries, and in Russia it has sometimes been almost persecuted as an innovation. It flourished especially in the famous Kozelski Optin Monastery. When and how it was introduced into our monastery I cannot say. There had already been three such elders, and Zossima was the last of them. But he was almost dying of weakness and disease, and they had no one to take his place. For our monastery this was an important question, because until then it had not been distinguished by anything in particular. It had no relics of saints, no wonder-working ikons, no glorious traditions, no historical exploits. It had flourished and become famous all over Russia through its elders, and pilgrims had flocked from every part of the country, thousands of miles, to see and hear them.

What was such an elder? He was one who took your soul and your will into his own soul and will. When you choose an elder, you give up your own will and hand it over to him in complete submission, complete self-denial. You take on this novitiate, this terrible school of self-denial, of your own free will. You hope to conquer and master yourself, so that after a life of obedience you may reach perfect freedom, that is, freedom from self. You hope to escape the fate of those who have lived their whole lives without finding their true selves in themselves. This institution of elders is not founded on theory. It grew up in the East out of a thousand years of practice. What is owed to an elder is not the ordinary “obedience” that has always existed in our Russian monasteries. It involves confession to the elder by all who have submitted to him, and an unbreakable bond between him and them.

The story is told, for instance, that in the early days of Christianity there was a novice who failed to carry out some command his elder had given him. He left his monastery in Syria and went to Egypt. There, after great exploits, he was at last found worthy to suffer torture and a martyr’s death for the faith. The Church regarded him as a saint. As they were burying him, the deacon called out, “Depart, all you unbaptized,” and suddenly the coffin with the martyr’s body left its place and was thrown out of the church. This happened three times. Only then did they learn that this holy man had broken his vow of obedience and left his elder. So, in spite of his great deeds, he could not be forgiven without the elder’s absolution. Only after that could the funeral take place. This, of course, is only an old legend. But here is a recent instance.

A monk was suddenly ordered by his elder to leave Athos, which he loved as a sacred place and a haven of refuge. He was to go first to Jerusalem, to pay homage to the Holy Places, and then north to Siberia: “There is the place for you, and not here.” The monk, overwhelmed with sorrow, went to the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople and begged to be released from his obedience. But the Patriarch replied that he could not release him. There was not, and could not be, any power on earth able to release him, except the elder who had himself laid that duty on him. In this way the elders are given, in certain cases, unlimited and inexplicable authority. That is why in many of our monasteries the institution was at first resisted almost to the point of persecution. Meanwhile the elders at once began to be highly esteemed among the people. Crowds of ignorant people, and men of distinction as well, flocked to the elders of our monastery, for instance, to confess their doubts, their sins and their sufferings, and to ask for counsel and admonition. Seeing this, the opponents of the elders declared that the sacrament of confession was being arbitrarily and frivolously degraded. Yet the monk’s or layman’s continual opening of his heart to the elder had nothing of the character of the sacrament. In the end, however, the institution of elders has been kept, and it is becoming established in Russian monasteries. It is true, perhaps, that this instrument, which had stood the test of a thousand years as a means of moral regeneration from slavery to freedom and to moral perfection, may be a two-edged weapon. It may lead some not to humility and complete self-control but to the most Satanic pride, that is, to bondage and not to freedom.

The elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a family of landowners and in his early youth had been in the army, serving as an officer in the Caucasus. No doubt he had impressed Alyosha by some peculiar quality of his soul. Alyosha lived in the elder’s cell. The elder was very fond of him and let him wait on him. It should be noted that Alyosha was bound by no obligation and could go where he pleased and be away for whole days. He wore the monastic dress voluntarily, so as not to be different from the others, and no doubt he liked wearing it. Possibly his youthful imagination was deeply stirred by the power and fame of his elder. It was said that over the years so many people had come to confess their sins to Father Zossima, and to beg him for words of advice and healing, that he had acquired the keenest insight. From an unfamiliar face he could tell what a newcomer wanted and what was torturing his conscience. He sometimes astounded and almost alarmed his visitors by knowing their secrets before they had spoken a word.

Alyosha saw that many people, almost all of them, entered the elder’s cell for the first time anxious and uneasy, yet left with bright, happy faces. What struck him most was that Father Zossima was not stern at all. He was nearly always cheerful. The monks used to say that he felt drawn to the more sinful, and the bigger the sinner, the more he loved him. No doubt there were some monks who hated and envied him, and they went on doing so to the end of his life. But there were few of them, and they kept quiet, though a few were men of real standing in the monastery. One was an older monk, famous for keeping strict fasts and vows of silence. Still, most of the monks were on Father Zossima’s side, and a great many loved him with all their hearts, warmly and sincerely. Some were devoted to him almost to the point of fanaticism. They said, not quite aloud, that he was a saint, that this was beyond doubt. Seeing that his end was near, they looked forward to miracles and great glory for the monastery before long, from his relics. Alyosha believed in the elder’s miraculous power without a shadow of doubt, just as he believed without a shadow of doubt in the story of the coffin that flew out of the church. He saw many people come with sick children or relatives and beg the elder to lay his hands on them and pray over them. Soon afterward, some of them the very next day, they returned and fell weeping at the elder’s feet to thank him for healing their sick.

Whether they had truly been healed or had merely got better as the illness ran its natural course was a question that did not exist for Alyosha. He had complete faith in his teacher’s spiritual power, and he rejoiced in the elder’s fame and glory as if it were his own triumph. His heart pounded, and he fairly shone all over, whenever the elder came out through the hermitage gates to the crowd of humbler pilgrims waiting there. They had come from every part of Russia for the sole purpose of seeing the elder and receiving his blessing. They threw themselves down before him, wept, kissed his feet, kissed the ground where he stood, and wailed. The women held their children up to him and brought him the sick who were “possessed with devils.” The elder spoke to them, read a short prayer over them, blessed them and sent them away. Recently he had grown so weak with his illness that sometimes he could not leave his cell, and the pilgrims would wait for days for him to appear. Alyosha did not wonder why they loved him so much, or why they fell down before him and wept with emotion at the mere sight of his face. Oh, he understood! The humble soul of the Russian peasant is worn out by grief and toil, and still more by the endless injustice and endless sin, his own and the world’s. For that soul it was the greatest need and comfort to find someone or something holy to fall down before and worship.

“Among us there is sin, injustice, and temptation. But still, somewhere on earth, there is someone holy and exalted. He has the truth; he knows the truth. So the truth is not dead upon the earth, and it will come one day to us too and rule over all the earth, as was promised.”

Alyosha knew that this was just how the people felt, and even how they reasoned. He understood it. But that the elder Zossima was this saint, this guardian of God’s truth—of that he had no more doubt than the weeping peasants and the sick women holding out their children to the elder. His conviction that the elder would bring extraordinary glory to the monastery after his death was even stronger than anyone else’s there. And lately a deep flame of inner ecstasy had been burning more and more strongly in his heart. It did not trouble him at all that this elder stood before him as a solitary example.

“No matter. He is holy. In his heart he carries the secret of renewal for everyone. He carries the power that will at last establish truth on the earth, so that all men will be holy and love one another, and there will be no more rich and poor, no high and low, but all will be like children of God, and the true Kingdom of Christ will come.” That was the dream in Alyosha’s heart.

The arrival of his two brothers, whom he had never known before, seemed to affect Alyosha deeply. He became friends with his half-brother Dmitri sooner than with his own brother Ivan, although Dmitri arrived later. Alyosha was extremely interested in Ivan. But Ivan had now been two months in the town, and though the two had met fairly often, they were still not close. Alyosha was silent by nature, and he seemed to be waiting for something and ashamed of something. Ivan, he had noticed, had at first looked at him long and with curiosity, but soon seemed to have stopped thinking about him. Alyosha noticed this with some embarrassment. At first he blamed his brother’s indifference on the gap in their ages and education. But he also wondered whether Ivan’s lack of curiosity and sympathy had some other cause altogether, one he knew nothing about. He kept fancying that Ivan was absorbed in something inward and important, that he was struggling toward some goal, perhaps a very difficult one, and that this was why he had no thought to spare for him. Alyosha wondered, too, whether the learned atheist might feel some contempt for him, a foolish novice. He knew for certain that his brother was an atheist. If there was contempt, he could not take offense at it. Yet, in an uneasy embarrassment that he did not understand himself, he waited for his brother to come nearer. Dmitri spoke of Ivan with the deepest respect and a peculiar earnestness. From Dmitri, Alyosha learned every detail of the important affair that had lately drawn the two elder brothers together in such a close and remarkable bond. Dmitri’s warm words about Ivan struck Alyosha all the more because Dmitri was, beside Ivan, almost uneducated. And the two brothers were such opposites in personality and character that it would be hard to find two men less alike.

It was at this time that the meeting, or rather the gathering, of this ill-matched family took place in the cell of the elder, who had such an extraordinary influence over Alyosha. The pretext for it was a false one. The quarrel between Dmitri and his father seemed to be at its worst just then, and relations between them had become unbearably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to propose, apparently as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima’s cell, and that, without appealing to his direct intervention, they might come to an understanding more decently under the soothing influence of the elder’s presence. Dmitri had never seen the elder. He naturally supposed that his father was trying to intimidate him. But he secretly blamed himself for losing his temper with his father several times lately, and so he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that he did not stay with his father, as Ivan did, but lived apart at the other end of the town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at that time, seized eagerly on the idea. He was a Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and an atheist, and he may have been driven by boredom or by the hope of some idle amusement. Suddenly he wanted to see the monastery and the holy man. His lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, and he made that his excuse to call on the Superior and try to settle it on friendly terms. A visitor with such praiseworthy intentions might get a warmer, more attentive reception than one who came out of simple curiosity. Pressure was put on the elder from inside the monastery. He had hardly left his cell lately, and illness had forced him to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he agreed to see them, and the day was set.
“Who made me a judge over them?” was all he said to Alyosha, smiling.

Alyosha was deeply troubled when he heard about the planned visit. Of all that quarrelsome, bickering company, Dmitri was the only one who could treat the meeting seriously. All the others would come with frivolous motives, which might even insult the elder. Alyosha knew that very well. Ivan and Miüsov would come out of curiosity, perhaps of the coarsest kind, and his father might be planning some piece of buffoonery. Alyosha said nothing, but he understood his father through and through. The boy, I repeat, was far from being as simple as everyone took him to be. He waited for the day with a heavy heart. No doubt he was forever turning over in his mind how the family discord might be ended. But his main worry was for the elder. He trembled for him and for his glory. He dreaded any insult to him, above all the refined, polite irony of Miüsov and the supercilious half-remarks of the highly educated Ivan. He even wanted to take the risk of warning the elder and telling him something about them, but on second thought he said nothing. He only sent a message the day before, through a friend, to his brother Dmitri, saying that he loved him and expected him to keep his promise. Dmitri was puzzled, because he could not remember what he had promised. He answered by letter that he would do his utmost not to be provoked “by vileness.” But although he had a deep respect for the elder and for his brother Ivan, he was convinced that the meeting was either a trap for him or an unworthy farce.
“All the same, I would rather bite out my tongue than fail in respect to the holy man you revere so highly,” he wrote in closing. The letter did not cheer Alyosha much.
